paras: The attempted lynching of Bailey was a night visit in September 1888 by friends of a Black man whom Bailey, an overseer in Crawford County, Arkansas, had shot and killed about a week earlier. The group fled when Bailey came out with a shotgun, and no one was hurt. The only known report, a short state-news item, presented the episode as an anecdote about the rope the would-be lynchers left behind.

According to the Forrest City Times, Bailey shot and killed a man described as "a negro" who, the paper said, "was trying to steal some cotton." A jury then exonerated Bailey "on the ground of self-defense." Neither the dead man nor Bailey's first name is given, and no town is named.

On a Sunday night after the jury's finding, "friends of the dead negro" came to Bailey's home and called him out, in the paper's words "with the evident intention of lynching him." When Bailey appeared holding a double-barreled shotgun, the group ran, leaving about thirty yards of new rope in his yard. The next morning Bailey used the rope as a well rope, remarking that they had saved him the expense of buying one.
No arrests of the men who came for Bailey, and no further proceedings over the shooting, appear in the coverage.

The episode survives in a single brief in the "Arkansas State News" column of the Forrest City Times of 29 September 1888, set among items on railroads, church buildings and a separate Crawford County killing. The item gave no source and took the theft accusation and the self-defense finding as settled, describing the dead man only as "a negro." It ended on Bailey's joke about the rope rather than on the killing, treating the failed attempt as a curiosity.
No Black-press coverage is available for 1888, and no other white paper carrying the story was found.

accounts.label: State-news brief (Forrest City Times)
accounts.gist: Bailey killed a Black man who was trying to steal cotton, was cleared by a jury on self-defense, and then scared off the dead man's friends, who had come to lynch him and left their rope behind.

framing.detail: The brief accepts the theft accusation and self-defense finding as fact, calls the dead man 'a negro', and closes on Bailey's joke that the would-be lynchers had saved him the cost of a well rope.
